did_you_know.text: The psalm’s title identifies it as a “Maskil”—a psalm with an instructional or contemplative character—and attributes it to Ethan the Ezrahite.

The psalm opens with a resolve to sing of the Lord’s lovingkindness forever and to proclaim his faithfulness from generation to generation, presenting faith as a mission passed down through the generations.
At the heart of the psalm is the covenant with David: the Lord is described as having made a covenant with his chosen one and sworn to David, his servant.
The psalmist describes the heavens and the assembly of the holy ones as acknowledging the Lord’s wonders and faithfulness, emphasizing that no one among the sons of gods is like him.
The sea serves in the psalm as a symbol of raging power over which the Lord rules; he is described as calming its waves and subduing Rahab.
The verse presents the foundations of the Lord’s kingship in the words “righteousness and justice,” accompanied by “lovingkindness and truth” going before him.
David is described as one whom the Lord found, anointed with his holy oil, and established as a mighty warrior and a chosen youth from among the people.

The covenant with David’s house also includes moral responsibility: if his descendants forsake the Lord’s law, they will be punished, but this does not cancel the Lord’s lovingkindness or his faithfulness to the covenant.

At this point the tone changes: after describing the promises to David, the psalmist portrays rejection, the destruction of fortifications, defeat, and the king’s humiliation—creating a cry over the gap between promise and reality.
Despite the dispute and lament, the psalm ends with a blessing to the Lord forever and a double conclusion: “Amen and amen.”
